name: barton-nackman
intent: Define an entire operator family once, in a shared carrier - classically a CRTP mixin base whose in-class friend functions are found by argument-dependent lookup - so that each member of a related family of types supplies only the primitive operation and inherits the complete, symmetrical operator set. In C++20 and later, defaulted comparisons and concepts often make the carrier unnecessary for ordinary value types; retain it for legacy targets, non-relational families or deliberately heterogeneous operators.
problem: A family of value-like types needs the same operator vocabulary (== and !=, the four relational operators, sometimes arithmetic), and writing each operator for each type means the derived operators drift apart, operand symmetry is lost when one operand becomes a member function's this pointer, and namespace-scope operator templates either apply too broadly or collide with each other under pre-C++20 overload-resolution rules. For ordinary member-wise value types, C++20 defaulted comparisons and semantic concepts remove most of this boilerplate, but they do not replace custom non-relational or heterogeneous families.
context: Compile-time, value-semantics code where several types share one operator vocabulary and one or two primitive operations can generate the rest: strong typedefs and domain value types, numeric, money and quantity types, and library code that must serve pre-C++20 toolchains or wants operator subsets (equality without ordering) and heterogeneous comparison. The same design decision reappears in other languages wherever one carrier can donate an operator family - protocol default implementations, module mixins, type classes or a derives clause.
benefits: One definition per operator serves the whole family: the derived operators (the companion comparisons, or the arithmetic suite derived from a compound primitive) are written once and stay mutually consistent instead of being duplicated per type.

Symmetry and conversions: the injected operators are non-members taking two operands of the family type, so both sides receive the same implicit conversions and the this-pointer asymmetry of member operators disappears.

Type-restricted, unambiguous resolution: each instantiation injects a genuine non-template function for one concrete type, which outranks any general operator template and cannot accidentally apply to unrelated types (the 'restricted' of restricted template expansion).
The operator set is opt-in and composable: a type can inherit equality only, equality plus ordering, or a full arithmetic suite, so it advertises exactly the operations it supports.
No runtime cost: the injected operators are inline, non-virtual functions, so the family gains the syntax and symmetry with no vtable, no allocation and no indirect call.

Semantic contracts can be expressed separately from generation: C++20 std::equality_comparable, std::totally_ordered and std::regular constrain what a family member must model, while the carrier remains an optional implementation technique rather than the contract itself.
tradeoffs: The operators are deliberately hidden: an injected friend is invisible to ordinary and qualified name lookup, so ::operator==(a, b) is ill-formed, code search and IDEs miss the definitions, and diagnostics point at the mixin header rather than at the family member.

The definition site is coupled to the mixin: the operator bodies must live inside the class template (that is what makes them friends), so the operator implementation cannot be moved to a separate translation unit or separated from the base template.

Overload-resolution risk: adding the mixin changes the candidate set of existing call sites, because the non-template friend participates in conversions on both operands and can hijack expressions that previously selected a different overload (the std::string/StringRef ambiguity removed in C++20 is the standard-library example).
One injected function per (type, operator) pair per instantiation: wide families multiply code size and template-error text, and every family member re-instantiates the mixin base.

It retires badly for common relational value types: C++20 defaulted operator<=> synthesises the relational family and C++20 concepts such as std::regular and std::equality_comparable describe the semantic contract for generic code; retaining a BN carrier then adds machinery without improving the algorithm's constraints. Keep it for legacy, non-relational, or heterogeneous families.

Compile-time only: whichever carrier is used, the operators resolve against the static type (ADL, conformance, implicit instance), so the operators are not virtual and comparing through a base-class reference compares the base subobject rather than the dynamic type.

Lookup is subtle in wrappers and dependent code: a namespace-scope operator template can fail deduction for std::reference_wrapper<T>, while a hidden non-template friend is found through the wrapped T's associated classes; manual qualified lookup still bypasses ADL. Test the actual generic wrapper instead of assuming every lookup path is equivalent.

participants.responsibility: Defines the operator family once as in-class friend functions parameterised on the family member (EqualityComparable<Derived>, Comparable<Derived>, TotallyOrdered<Derived>, or the protocol/module/trait equivalent); it holds no state and exists only to donate the operators.

Supplies the primitive operation(s) the family is derived from (equalTo, compare or operator<, or the compound arithmetic primitive) and inherits the carrier; as the CRTP argument it makes each injected function concrete.
The one or two hand-written operations that carry the semantics (classically == and <); every other operator is expressed in terms of them, so semantic consistency is decided here.
The generated overloads - one concrete non-template, non-member function per (instantiation, operator) - defined inside the class template and injected when it is instantiated.

Finds the injected operators because the operand type's associated classes include the mixin base, so the expression a == b resolves without any namespace-scope declaration and qualified lookup cannot see them.

use_cases: Value types and strong typedefs (Money, Meter, Version, Id) that must support equality and a total order everywhere they appear, including as keys of ordered containers.

Numeric and quantity types - matrices, vectors, big integers, fixed-point decimals, units of measure - where a full arithmetic operator family is expected as syntax and can be derived from a few primitives (compound assignment, addition, equality).
Heterogeneous comparison in a library API: comparing a family member with a scalar or with a sibling representation without writing mirrored operator overloads for both operand orders.

Opting into a partial operator set: equality-comparable but not ordered, ordered but not arithmetic, or iterators and containers composed from the same mechanism (the operator groups of Boost.Operators).

Cross-language equivalents where one protocol, module, trait or decorator donates the operator family - Ruby's Comparable, Swift's Comparable protocol defaults, Scala's Ordered/Ordering, Python's functools.total_ordering.

Customising swap for a type: injecting a hidden-friend void swap(T&, T&) noexcept enables std::ranges::swap and std::swap both to find it via ADL, giving zero-cost, type-specific swap without polluting any namespace.

Making a type work through std::reference_wrapper in generic algorithms: a hidden-friend operator (BN style) is found by ADL when algorithms indirectly hold the type via reference_wrapper; a free-function template operator is not found because template deduction requires an exact type match rather than a reference-like wrapper.

Exposing operator customisation to std::ranges without polluting the enclosing namespace: the hidden friend lives in the type's associated namespace and is found exclusively by ADL, which std::ranges uses internally for its customisation points.

Boost.Operators (<boost/operators.hpp>) is the canonical library carrier: equality_comparable, less_than_comparable, addable and two-argument forms derive grouped operators from a small primitive set.

Boost.Iterator's iterator_facade<Derived,...> is a production CRTP carrier for iterator comparisons, arithmetic, dereference and increment: an iterator supplies core operations while the facade publishes the standard interface.

Boost.Numeric.Odeint custom state types: the documented point3D chains boost::additive1, boost::additive2 and boost::multiplicative2 as CRTP bases and hand-writes only operator+= and operator*=, letting the injected operators supply the full arithmetic vocabulary the library's vector_space_algebra steppers call.

Boost.Operators is itself a shipped production carrier: boost/operators.hpp defines less_than_comparable, equality_comparable, totally_ordered and the arithmetic mixins as CRTP bases whose in-class friend operators (implicitly inline per [class.friend]) take an empty_base chaining parameter for the empty-base optimisation, and since the 2016 'ADL protection' revision (Daniel Frey) the carriers live in boost::operators_impl, so the injected operators are reachable only via ADL on the operand's base classes, not as boost::operator<=.
avoid_when: A single type with two or three operators: writing them directly is shorter and far easier to debug than a template mixin.
C++20 or later with member-wise ordering: a defaulted operator<=> (which also generates operator==) produces the relational family with no mixin at all.
The language cannot define operators for user-defined types (C, Go, JavaScript, TypeScript): use named functions or methods instead of simulating operators with macros and coercions.

The comparison must be virtual or depend on the dynamic type: operators resolve statically, so polymorphic comparison needs equals/compareTo-style virtual methods (Java's Comparable, C#'s IComparable) instead.

Comparison semantics differ per call site (several legitimate orderings of one type): an operator set baked into the type fixes one ordering; use a comparator abstraction (Comparator, Ordering, an explicit comparison function) instead.
You need to call operators with qualified lookup (::operator==(a, b)): injected hidden friends are found only by ADL and qualified calls silently fail to find them.

The goal is only to constrain generic algorithms: std::regular, std::equality_comparable and std::totally_ordered state semantic requirements but do not generate operators; define or default the operations directly and constrain the algorithm instead.
anti_patterns: Confusing the idiom with CRTP itself: the Barton-Nackman trick is a distinct technique that happens to be built on CRTP, so 'we use CRTP' says nothing about whether operators are injected or found only by ADL.

Using namespace std::rel_ops as a substitute: it injects four operator templates into every translation unit that includes it, defines != and > as the negation of <, and was deprecated in C++20. It is unbounded and applies to all types, defeating the 'restricted' in restricted template expansion.

Writing namespace-scope operator templates that convert both operands (template <class T> bool operator==(const T&, const T&)) and calling that a mixin: the template is unbounded, applies to unrelated types, and discards the restricted, type-specific resolution the idiom exists for.

Mixing a generated operator family with a hand-written operator of the same name but different semantics (mixin == beside a custom < that ignores a field): the family's consistency contract breaks and ordered containers disagree with equality.
Using the carrier to make semantically unrelated types comparable - a 'family' by convenience rather than by meaning - so that expressions compile which should never have been written.

Defining operators as free-function templates in the type's namespace (e.g., template<class V> bool operator<(const Cat<V>&, const Cat<V>&)): unlike hidden-friend non-templates, these require exact type matching for template argument deduction, so they fail when generic algorithms wrap the type in std::reference_wrapper or other indirection. Barton-Nackman's non-template friend is found via ADL regardless of wrapper types.
design_principles: Do not repeat yourself: one definition per operator, parameterised over the family, instead of one definition per (operator, type) pair.
Interface segregation: a family member opts into exactly the operator subsets it supports (equality only, ordered, arithmetic) rather than one monolithic comparable interface.
Symmetry: operations on two operands of the same type belong to non-member functions so both sides convert alike.

Information hiding by construction: the operators are reachable only through the operands' associated types, keeping the type's interface free of scope-level declarations (the aspect that later became known as hidden friends).
Open/closed: a new family member joins by implementing the primitive and inheriting the carrier, never by editing the operator definitions.

ADL-only visibility: the injected operators must not be reachable by qualified or ordinary unqualified lookup; they live in the type's associated namespace and are discovered only when the type appears as an operand — this is what makes the pattern work with std::reference_wrapper and std::ranges.
best_practices: Choose the operator subset the type can honestly support; do not inherit a total-ordering mixin for a type whose < defines only a strict weak ordering, and keep the derived operators' semantics consistent with equality.
Keep the primitive operations (==, <, or the compound arithmetic primitive) hand-written, small and total: every injected operator inherits their edge cases.

Prefer the hidden-friend form (operators defined inside the class, found by ADL) over namespace-scope operator templates, so the overload set stays type-restricted and does not grow for unrelated code. This also enables std::reference_wrapper-based generic algorithms to find the operators.

On C++20 and later use defaulted operator<=> for member-wise ordering and reserve the mixin for pre-C++20 targets, non-relational operator families, heterogeneous comparison, and cases where the default lexicographic ordering does not match the domain semantics.

Prefer Boost.Operators (or an equivalent hand-rolled equivalent) for pre-C++20 code: it provides tested, composable mixins (equality_comparable, less_than_comparable, addable, etc.) with optional base-class chaining to keep object size minimal through empty-base optimisation.

Match the carrier to the language - protocol default implementations, module mixins, traits/type classes, decorators - instead of hand-writing the same operator set per type in a language that has a carrier.

Test the operator suite explicitly (both operand orders, implicit conversions, the equality and ordering axioms, use through std::reference_wrapper in std::sort): the injected operators are invisible to code search, so nothing else will notice a missing or inconsistent one.

Inject a hidden-friend swap for any type with non-trivial resources: friend void swap(T&, T&) noexcept found via ADL is the idiomatic way to enable std::ranges::swap and std::swap to find the type-specific overload without any namespace pollution.

In C++23, prefer deducing this (void foo(this const T&)) over CRTP for mixin-style operators: it achieves the same static polymorphism without the curiously recurring template argument and produces cleaner error messages.

Never use std::rel_ops in new code: it is deprecated, namespace-polluting, and type-unrestricted. Its only advantage over hand-written operators is brevity, which is not worth the semantic and compile-time costs.
pitfalls: Qualified calls cannot find injected friends: ::operator==(a, b) is always ill-formed for a hidden-friend operator; only unqualified calls trigger ADL and find it. Document this in code reviews.

ADL-dependent context stripping: when a type passes through another template (e.g., std::reference_wrapper<T>, std::optional<T>, a proxy iterator), the associated namespaces used for ADL may not include the namespace where the friend was injected. In practice, BN non-template friends are found correctly in these cases, but code that manually searches the type's namespace without ADL will miss them.

One-definition-rule risk: because the injected friend originates from a template, it is implicitly inline. Providing diverging in-class definitions in different translation units (e.g., through partial specialisation with conflicting friends for the same type) is undefined behaviour with no guaranteed diagnostic.

Reference-wrapper incompatibility with free-function templates: STL containers such as std::vector and std::sort use free-function template operators (e.g., template<class V> bool operator<(const Cat<V>&, const Cat<V>&)). These require exact template argument deduction, so they fail when the algorithm wraps elements in reference_wrapper or similar indirection. Barton-Nackman hidden-friend non-template operators do not have this problem and are found correctly.

Combining BN with defaulted operator<=> on C++20: if a type both inherits a BN mixin and declares operator<=> = default, the compiler may produce conflicting operator definitions. Keep the two mechanisms separate or use one exclusively.

Private-constructor protection can break mixin chaining: some implementations make the mixin's constructors private and befriend the derived type. This prevents the mixin from being used as a base class by anything other than the intended derived type, which is intentional but can surprise generic code that tries to reuse the mixin.

Use std::regular as if it generated operator== -> the concept only checks copy/default/equality expressions and the type fails when no equality operator exists -> define or default equality first, then use the concept to constrain clients.

Inherit a total-ordering carrier for a type whose domain has incomparable values (NaN, a pre-release version, or a unit mismatch) -> derived <= and >= can assume false trichotomy and disagree with equality -> use a partial-order primitive or an explicit comparator instead.

Replace a heterogeneous BN family with one defaulted operator<=> -> the default compares only the declared class and its members, so scalar or sibling operands still fail -> add explicit heterogeneous comparisons or retain a narrowly scoped carrier.

Wrong move: reach for an injected operator through a qualified call (boost::operator<=(a, b) or ::operator<=(a, b)) -> hidden friends are invisible to ordinary and qualified lookup, and Boost.Operators' ADL-protection rewrite moved its carriers into boost::operators_impl, so the qualified call does not compile even though a <= b works -> call the operator unqualified and rely on ADL through the operand's associated classes.

Wrong move: expose a public numeric type through the heterogeneous two-operand Boost.Operators mixins (equality_comparable2, less_than_comparable2) without constraining the foreign operand -> the mirrored overloads accept nonsense: Boost.Rational's header records that rational<int> r; r == 3.5 compiled and passed under the derived suite -> constrain each mixed-type pair (enable_if pre-C++20, concepts after) or hand-write the heterogeneous operators, which is what Boost.Rational did when it retired the derived suite.

Wrong move: port pre-C++98 Barton-Nackman advice (Barton & Nackman 1994; C++ Templates section 11.7) that the inline friend injects the operator name into the enclosing or global scope -> friend name injection was removed from the standard, so the injected name is not visible to ordinary unqualified lookup and any code relying on scope-level visibility fails -> treat ADL through associated classes as the only guaranteed discovery mechanism, and remember the idiom is distinct from CRTP (it often rides on a CRTP base but does not require one).
sources: Barton, J. J. & Nackman, L. R., Scientific and Engineering C++: An Introduction with Advanced Techniques and Examples (Addison-Wesley, 1994) - the idiom's origin, originally named restricted template expansion, introduced to define operators for class templates on pre-standard compilers that lacked function template overloading.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barton%E2%80%93Nackman_trick
https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/More_C%2B%2B_Idioms/Barton-Nackman_trick

https://open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/1996/N0878.pdf — ISO C++ WG21 paper N0878: An Alternative to Name Injection from Templates, documenting the C++98 adjustment from friend name injection to ADL.

https://www.boost.org/latest/libs/utility/doc/html/utility/utilities/operators.html — Boost.Operators library, the canonical implementation of Barton-Nackman in the C++ standard-library ecosystem, providing equality_comparable, less_than_comparable, addable, and composable grouped operator templates.

https://bigcpp.com/reference/idioms/barton-nackman — bigcpp.com comprehensive reference covering the mechanism, C++20 comparison with operator<=> (including the reference_wrapper compatibility issue), friend name injection history, and a feature comparison table.

https://brevzin.github.io/c%2B%2B/2019/07/28/comparisons-cpp20/ — Barry Revzin's C++20 comparisons blog, explaining primary vs. secondary operators, the rewrite rules for operator<=>, defaulted spaceship, and why only primary operators need to be written.

https://www.fluentcpp.com/2019/04/09/how-to-emulate-the-spaceship-operator-before-c20-with-crtp/ — Jonathan Boccara (Fluent C++), comparing TieComparable CRTP mixin with IneqComparable, showing performance trade-offs and non-lexical comparison use cases.

https://quuxplusone.github.io/blog/2020/12/09/barton-nackman-in-practice/ — Arthur O'Dwyer, practical demonstration that BN hidden-friend operators work correctly with std::reference_wrapper in std::sort while free-function template operators fail due to template deduction constraints.

https://hackingcpp.com/cpp/lang/adl.html — Hacking C++ ADL ultimate guide, covering Niebloids, hidden-friend mechanics, ADL suppression, and why hidden friends protect against accidental implicit conversions.

https://www.justsoftwaresolutions.co.uk/cplusplus/hidden_friends.html — Just Software Solutions, detailed explanation of hidden friend discovery rules and how they compose with strong typedefs and enum wrappers.

https://www.modernescpp.com/ — Modernes C++ (Rainer Grimm), authoritative coverage of hidden friends, ADL customisation points, and the evolution of operator overloading idioms through C++98 to C++20.

https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/language/default_comparisons — cppreference page on C++20 default comparisons, documenting defaulted operator<=> and its synthesis of operator==, plus the rewrite rules for secondary comparison operators.

https://www.boost.org/latest/libs/iterator/doc/html/iterator_facade.html — Boost.Iterator iterator_facade, a production CRTP facade that supplies standard iterator operations from derived core primitives.

https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/concepts/regular — cppreference definition of std::regular as semiregular plus equality_comparable; concepts constrain semantic contracts and do not synthesize operators.
https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/friend — cppreference friend-declaration reference covering friend definitions and lookup mechanics used by hidden-friend operators.

https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#c161-use-non-member-functions-for-symmetric-operators — C++ Core Guidelines C.161 recommendation for non-member symmetric operators, useful boundary guidance for generated operator families.

https://theboostcpplibraries.com/boost.operators — The Boost C++ Libraries, Chapter 72 Boost.Operators: deriving from boost::less_than_comparable gives a type operator>, operator<= and operator>= from a hand-written operator<, and boost::partially_ordered covers types whose operator< is not a total order.

https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/latest/libs/numeric/odeint/doc/html/boost_numeric_odeint/odeint_in_detail/state_types__algebras_and_operations.html — Boost.Numeric.Odeint official documentation: the custom point3D state type chains boost::additive1, boost::additive2 and boost::multiplicative2 so operator+= and operator*= alone supply the operator family the vector_space_algebra steppers require.

https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/language/friend_name_injection — cppreference on friend name injection: the Barton-Nackman trick originally relied on friend name injection before it was removed from the standard; modern discovery is ADL.

https://0-1.at/w3-home/errata_bn.html — errata to C++ Templates section 11.7 (Thomas Schell): the Barton-Nackman trick is not CRTP and does not necessarily involve it; it was invented to inject a non-member function via an inline friend definition when function templates could not be overloaded.

https://github.com/boostorg/rational/blob/develop/include/boost/rational.hpp — Boost.Rational source and changelog: the operator suite was historically derived from Boost.Operators ('Use _left versions of operators from operators.hpp'), then hand-rewritten as constrained non-member overloads because the derived suite allowed rational == 3.5 to compile and pass.

related_patterns_notes.crtp: crtp (the static-polymorphism mechanism used by the carrier; it is broader than operator-family generation)
related_patterns_notes.traits: traits (describe capabilities; unlike Barton-Nackman, a trait does not itself inject operators)
related_patterns_notes.policy-based-design: policy-based-design (composes selectable behavior; BN is a fixed operator-family policy for a self type)
related_patterns_notes.non-copyable-mixin: non-copyable-mixin (a mixin controlling copying; it does not derive symmetric operators)
related_patterns_notes.empty-base-optimization: empty-base-optimization (can remove storage cost of the empty carrier; it does not provide the operator semantics)
related_patterns_notes.tag-dispatching: tag-dispatching (selects overloads from type tags at call sites; BN creates type-associated operators)
related_patterns_notes.value-object: value-object (the semantic target of coherent equality/order; BN is only a generation mechanism)
related_patterns_notes.hidden-friend: hidden-friend (the lookup/access technique used by BN; it can be used without CRTP)
related_patterns_notes.speculative-constexpr: speculative-constexpr (an unrelated compile-time evaluation technique; it does not generate operator families)
